text: fail2ban doesn't inspect network traffic directly — it watches log files. On Debian and Ubuntu that's auth.log; on RHEL and CentOS it's secure. A filter is a set of regex patterns describing what a failed login looks like in that log. When enough matching failures from the same source IP happen inside a configured window, fail2ban reacts by banning that IP at the firewall.

A jail is fail2ban's per-service configuration unit, defined in jail.local so it survives package upgrades. This sshd jail watches auth.log with the sshd filter: maxretry 5 means five failures trigger a ban, findtime 10 minutes is the window those failures have to land in, and bantime 1 hour is how long the resulting ban lasts before the IP can try again.

Trace the whole sequence end to end: a failed SSH login lands in the log, the jail's filter recognizes it as a match, enough matches accumulate inside the findtime window to cross maxretry, and fail2ban responds by inserting a firewall rule that drops every packet from that IP for the configured bantime — all without touching sshd's own configuration, and without the attacker's script getting any indication of why its connections suddenly stopped landing.

fail2ban-client status lists every active jail; adding a jail name, like status sshd, shows that jail's current ban list specifically. set sshd unbanip followed by an address lifts a ban immediately, which matters when a legitimate user, or your own second laptop, gets caught by the threshold and needs back in before the ban expires on its own.

Even with keys-only SSH already in place, fail2ban still earns its spot: it's defense in depth against a future misconfiguration, it protects any other service with a matchable failure pattern, from a web login form to FTP, and it keeps connection-flood noise from piling up in the logs you're already reviewing.
